images.caption:
The Folly Theater at 9th and C Streets, NW shortly before its demolition, 5/12/29 "Washington Post" ("A Once-Popular Playhouse Passes", p. 3,  which gives a history of the theater.)
The Folly was a vaudeville house that had several names during its lifetime (1850-1929), including Ford's Opera House, The Bijou, and The Majestic.  

Another shot of this building.

images.caption:
Bethany Chapel, on the corner of Thirteenth and C Streets, NW, in a drawing from the 8/15/03 Post.  A mission of New York Avenue Presbyterian Church, it was built in 1874 and appears to have been razed for the construction of Federal Triangle.

The chapel is also visible in this photo.  The site is now occupied by the Ronald Reagan Building.

images.caption:
Washington, mainly the Mall area, from the air.  This is the only good photo I have of Washington from an airplane, in the 22 years that I lived in the Washington area.  I have some photos from the top of the Washington Monument, which are almost as good.
The Washington Monument is in the right foreground.  The Capitol is at the far end of the Mall.  Constitution Avenue runs diagonally through the center of the photo.  The Federal Triangle is the red-roofed buildings left of Constitution Avenue.  The White House is hidden under the airplane wing, to the left of the grass circle.  My office at American Petroleum Institute (API) is also hidden by the wing, near where the edge of the wing meets the real edge of the photo.  
The first three buildings on the Mall, left of the Washington Monument, are the American History Museum, Natural History Museum, and National Gallery of Art (Mellon Gallery).  The Air and Space Museum is on the right side of the Mall, beyond the circular building.  

New York Avenue is the diagonal street at the upper left of the photo.  Robert F. Kennedy Stadium and the D.C. Armory are in the right background.

images.caption:
Three of Washington's most famous museums, on the north side of the Mall.  Museum of History and Technology was opened in 1964.  It was later renamed National Museum of American History.  The National Museum of Natural History was openin 1910.  Both museums are part of the Smithsonian Institution.  The view is looking ENE from the Washington Monument.
The National Gallery of Art was established in 1937 and opened in 1941.  It is often called the Mellon Gallery, after Andrew W. Mellon.  He donated his large collection of old masters and $10 million for the building.  The National Gallery of Art is not part of the Smithsonian Institution.  

Constitution Avenue separates the museums from the buildings in the "Federal Triangle."  These buildings were built and the early and mid 1930s.  The Senate Office Buildings are in the distance on Constitution Avenue.  Union Station is barely visible, below the source of the pillar of smoke and just to its left.

images.caption: Eastern Market, located at the intersection of 7th and C Streets, S.E., in the Capitol Hill neighborhood of Washington, D.C.  Built 1871–1873 to the designs of noted architect Adolf Cluss, Eastern Market is an example of Italianate architecture.  The building was listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) in 1971, and is designated as a contributing property to the Capitol Hill Historic District, listed on the NRHP in 1976.
